displayQuote: Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what people fear most

meta.title: Who really said "Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what people fear most"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Dostoevsky. It is Raskolnikov in Crime and Punishment (1866), Part 1, Chapter 1 — though Garnett's 1914 translation reads "what they fear most."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what people fear most'?
meta.ogDescription: Real, and traceable: Raskolnikov's interior monologue in Crime and Punishment, Part 1, Chapter 1. The "people" wording is a variant of Garnett's "they."

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. It is Raskolnikov thinking to himself in the opening chapter of Crime and Punishment, serialized in 1866 — and it survives in Constance Garnett’s 1914 English translation, which reads “what they fear most.” The popular wording swaps that “they” for “people” — a one-word variant of the same sentence. Dostoevsky’s Russian says “they” there too; it is the sentence immediately before that asks what people are most afraid of, which Garnett rendered as “men,” and the variant appears to have carried that noun forward.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Serialized in The Russian Messenger, January–December 1866; single volume 1867
Part I, Chapter I — Raskolnikov’s interior monologue

source.excerpt: “I want to attempt a thing like that and am frightened by these trifles,” he thought, with an odd smile. “Hm... yes, all is in a man’s hands and he lets it all slip from cowardice, that’s an axiom. It would be interesting to know what it is men are most afraid of. Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what they fear most.... But I am talking too much. It’s because I chatter that I do nothing.”
trail: Searched the primary text first. Project Gutenberg’s Crime and Punishment, translated by Constance Garnett ↗, carries the sentence in Part I, Chapter I: “It would be interesting to know what it is men are most afraid of. Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what they fear most.”
Confirmed it in print, not just in a digital transcription. A scanned Collier printing of the Garnett translation ↗ shows the same passage in the opening pages of Part I, Chapter I.

Checked the Russian. Dostoevsky’s original on Russian Wikisource ↗ reads «Любопытно, чего люди больше боятся? Нового шага, нового собственного слова они всего больше боятся» — «люди» (“people”) in the question, but «они» (“they”) in the sentence the popular wording actually quotes, which is what Garnett wrote.

Cross-checked the attribution. Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced Crime and Punishment section, not under Misattributed or Disputed, and marks “what people fear most” as a variant translation. Quote Investigator has no article on it.
source.excerptNote: Garnett’s 1914 translation reads “what they fear most” — and so does the Russian sentence behind it, «они всего больше боятся». The form that circulates online swaps in “people,” a word that belongs to the sentence just before — «чего люди больше боятся», which Garnett turned into “men.”

source.rightsNote: The novel was serialized in 1866 ↗ and Constance Garnett’s English translation — the one that carries this sentence — was published in 1914, so both the Russian original and this English wording are public domain in the United States. The single-word “people” variant is not traced to any named modern translator; if it were drawn from a specific later translation, that translation would carry its own copyright.

author.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Dostoevsky was arrested in 1849 for belonging to the Petrashevsky Circle, marched out to be shot, reprieved at the last moment by a letter from the tsar, and sent to a Siberian prison camp for four years of hard labour. He came back with the preoccupations that made him — guilt, freedom, the terrible cost of an idea taken seriously — and poured them into Crime and Punishment, which ran in twelve monthly installments through 1866. He is a writer people quote constantly and read carefully rather less often, which is exactly why lines like this one drift.

misattribution.heading: What drifted
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is sound — this is one of the rare viral Dostoevsky lines that really is Dostoevsky. What has drifted is the wording, and the fact that a character is saying it.

items.why: Constance Garnett’s 1914 translation, the one carried by Project Gutenberg ↗, reads “Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what they fear most.” Wikiquote ↗ records the “people” form as a variant translation and does not name a translator for it.

The Russian original ↗ reads «нового собственного слова» — a new word of one’s own. Garnett drops it, and the wording that circulates online follows her — though later renderings restore it: an essay for the North American Dostoevsky Society gives the line as “a new step, a new word of their own” ↗.

items.who: Raskolnikov, not Dostoevsky in his own voice
items.why: The sentence is a murderer’s self-justifying interior monologue in Part I, Chapter I, and he dismisses it himself two lines later: “But I am talking too much.” It circulates as motivational advice from the author, which inverts its meaning in the novel ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Dostoevsky wrote it, in Crime and Punishment, Part 1, Chapter 1 — but he gave it to Raskolnikov, and the canonical English wording is “what they fear most.” Read the passage ↗.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: The sentence is not Dostoevsky philosophizing in his own voice. It is Raskolnikov — broke, feverish, weeks into doing nothing but lying in his room and talking himself in circles — walking out into a hot July street in Petersburg and catching himself being frightened of his landlady while planning a murder. The thought about a new step and a new word is his excuse, dressed as an insight.

That framing is the whole point of the chapter. Raskolnikov immediately undercuts himself: “But I am talking too much. It’s because I chatter that I do nothing.” The novel spends six parts demonstrating what happens when a man decides his private theory entitles him to take that new step.
detailsBody: Dostoevsky’s Russian reads «Нового шага, нового собственного слова они всего больше боятся» — literally a new step, a new word of one’s own. Garnett renders it simply as “uttering a new word,” dropping «собственного».

The omission matters for the novel, because Raskolnikov later builds an entire theory on exactly that phrase — dividing humanity into the ordinary and the men who have, as Garnett puts it, “the gift or the talent to utter a new word.” The opening-chapter thought is the seed of the argument he uses to justify the killing.

sourcesVerified.claim: Project Gutenberg ebook #2554 is Crime and Punishment translated by Constance Garnett, and its text contains 'It would be interesting to know what it is men are most afraid of. Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what they fear most....' in Part I, Chapter I.

This Internet Archive item is a scanned printing of the Garnett translation of Crime and Punishment (creators listed as Dostoyevsky and Constance Black Garnett), and its OCR text contains 'Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what they fear most' in the opening pages of Part I, Chapter I.

Dostoevsky's Russian original of Part I, Chapter I reads «Любопытно, чего люди больше боятся? Нового шага, нового собственного слова они всего больше боятся…», confirming both 'люди' (people) and the word 'собственного' (of one's own) that Garnett omits.

Wikiquote lists the line under its sourced 'Crime and Punishment (1866)' section as 'Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what they fear most,' and adds 'Variant translation: Taking a new step, uttering a new word, is what people fear most.' It is not in the Misattributed or Disputed sections.

Crime and Punishment was first published in twelve monthly installments in the literary journal The Russian Messenger during 1866, issued as a single volume in 1867, and Constance Garnett's English translation was published in 1914.

Fyodor Dostoevsky lived 11 November 1821 to 9 February 1881, was a Russian novelist, short-story writer, essayist and journalist, joined the Petrashevsky Circle in 1846, was arrested in April 1849, had his death sentence commuted, and served four years of hard labour at a katorga prison camp in Omsk, Siberia.

Deborah A. Martinsen's essay for the North American Dostoevsky Society renders the Part I, Chapter I line as 'what do people fear most? A new step, a new word of their own,' preserving the «собственного» that Garnett drops — so the omission is Garnett's, not universal to English renderings.
Quote Investigator has no article investigating this Dostoevsky quotation; a site search for 'uttering a new word' returns only unrelated quotations.
